Why we changed
Other bots moved to their own page
Everything about how other Stoat bots handle your data, and what Stoat has said about the rules, now lives on its own page, so this one only covers what Stoatmod changed.
Removed images and uploaded files get a deadline

When Stoatmod removes an image, moderators can see what was removed behind a content warning. Graphic violence is kept only as a reduced copy. Explicit nudity is kept only as a small thumbnail that is permanently blurred, and the original is never stored. Images that may involve minors are never kept at all.
These copies are deleted with the case content 30 days after the decision, or when an appeal is decided.
Every uploaded file, including report evidence, case evidence and appeal attachments, is now deleted 30 days after upload unless an open appeal needs it.
Image scanning on by default
Image scanning now runs by default, on our own hardware like text moderation. It checks only for graphic gore and explicit nudity, and the image isn't kept unless it's removed.
Servers that had turned image scanning off kept their choice. Server owners can still turn it off for the whole server or for single channels.
Our code is public
We published the bot, the dashboard API and the website under AGPL-3.0, so anyone can check that Stoatmod does what this page says.
Older message text purged, and new features built to expire
The 30-day deletion rule now covers the message text in every kind of moderation record, not just AI decisions. Older records that still had message text were cleaned up the same day.
The optional Thinking check stores the AI's reasoning about a flagged message. It's off by default and deleted with the original message after 30 days.
Join protection, which stops new members posting links or attachments for a while, records only the server, the account and the start and end times, and deletes that record when protection ends.
The report form now loads Cloudflare Turnstile only after you agree to it, the same as join verification.

What we changed about privacy,

Every change Stoatmod has made to how it handles your data, newest first. It starts with the rebuild after Stoat's privacy review in October 2026 and carries on with everything since.
We've stopped using outside AI, IP checks, cross-server sharing and per-user stats. Everything we still keep, including removed images and uploaded files, has a deletion deadline.

03 / What we keep, and for how long
In line with Stoat's guidance

04 / What's still there

Join verification and the report form still use Cloudflare Turnstile as a browser CAPTCHA, but only after the person agrees: it doesn't load until they tick the agreement. Stoat has not objected to us continuing to use it where the person consents.

Our AI reads every message in the channels it moderates, and images too unless a server turns image scanning off. Stoat has said this is allowed without opt-in as long as nothing is kept after the check, which is how it works: only messages the AI acts on are kept, and only for the times above.
05 / Why we changed
Stoat reviewed Stoatmod, and we rebuilt it.

On 5 September 2026, Stoat Trust & Safety gave us 30 days to remove or redesign the parts of Stoatmod that collected or kept data without consent. The notice quoted Stoat's published Community Guidelines:
We made the October changes within that deadline, and we've kept going since. The full email chain shows exactly what Stoat asked of us.
What about other bots?
We think every bot should be held to the same rules.
We've looked at how AutoMod, Kuma, bronx, bolt, log_it and others handle your data, what's changed since, and what Stoat has said about the rules. That now has its own page.

06 / What happens next

Every future change to how Stoatmod handles your data will be added to the top of this page. We'll fix things when the evidence says we should, stick to our deletion deadlines and give you a real choice wherever consent is needed. When Stoat publishes its developer guidelines, we'll check Stoatmod against them and record what we change here.

Every message AutoMod sees, in every server, is printed with its full text to the bot's output, and nothing in the code turns this off. Under the Docker setup in AutoMod's self-hosting guide, that output would be saved to a log file with no size limit. AutoMod's developer has told us these logs are a debugging feature and aren't kept on the official instance.

AutoMod's support server carries Stoat's verified badge, its developer is on the Stoat team, and its README calls it "Stoat's premier moderation bot". Yet its website, docs and source code have no privacy policy, terms or privacy notice, so members can't find out what it collects, how long it keeps it or how to ask for deletion. Its developer told us in October that Stoat had asked for one and that it was being prepared with legal advice. As of 19 November it still hasn't been published.

Fixed on 14 October 2026 and still the case on 19 November. Kuma's November privacy policy says cross-server flagging is off for every Stoat community, and its commands page says Raid Guard isn't available on Stoat because Stoat's rules don't allow sharing raid flags between communities.

Kuma's Raid Guard "automatically isolates or kicks accounts that have been auto-flagged for raid/spam activity in other Kuma-protected communities". Privacy policy (updated November 2026)

Fixed on 14 October 2026 and still the case on 19 November. Kuma's privacy policy says there's no VPN or proxy check and no IP hashing on Stoat, and its commands page says Stoat servers never get IP, VPN or alt-linking checks.

Kuma's verification help text said that with "ip on" by default, a captcha-passer's connection was screened for VPN, proxy or high-risk IPs and same-network accounts were linked, using a hashed IP kept for 30 days.
Privacy policy: verification

A server owner can bridge a channel to Discord and Fluxer with !bridge. Kuma's privacy policy says it then copies members' messages, "their text, attachments, and your username and avatar", to the other platforms. Its November policy still describes bridging only as off until an admin sets it up. We found no notice to members, consent step or opt-out, so this raises the same consent question as bolt.
Privacy policy: cross-platform bridging

The bridge has three settings: whether @everyone mentions pass through, whether platform names are shown, and whether join codes expire. There's nothing that asks members for consent, tells them the channel is bridged or lets one person opt out. Its website and legal page still mention none, as of 19 November.

Someone can join a server, open a channel and start chatting without realising their messages, name and avatar are being reposted on another platform where Stoat's rules and deletion controls don't apply. Showing the platform name, such as "Joey (Stoat)", is off by default.

Each person's daily message, edit, delete and command counts are stored for every server and every channel until they opt out or the bot leaves. Stoat's guidance allows this kind of data to be kept that long, but says counts tied to a person are user data that need opt-in.

Anyone can run .stats top g to rank the most active people across every server bronx is in, even outside a server. People are ranked whether or not they've ever used bronx, unless they've opted out. bronx's homepage and README still advertise it. Stoat says cross-server rankings fall under a bot's general opt-in.

Application answers are stored with the applicant's user ID and no deletion deadline, and the privacy page still gives no retention period for them. Stoat's guidance says content like this should be kept for 30 days unless there's a specific reason to keep it longer. Stoatmod deletes applications after 14 days.

bronx's privacy page lets anyone download their data or opt out, which deletes their records and stops future tracking, and on 14 October bronx added the same opt-out to levels. But nobody is asked before counting starts, and Stoat has said it's asking every bot to use opt-in.

The privacy page still says "nothing is collected passively" and that data is only written when you use a feature. The code counts every message a person sends, whether or not they've ever used bronx.
A decision on bridge bots: whether members must be told, or asked, before their messages are copied to another platform.
Find its privacy policy

Look for a link on the bot's website or profile. It should say what's collected, why, who it's shared with, how long it's kept and how to ask for deletion. No policy at all is the biggest warning sign.
Check whether you're asked first
Stoat is asking bots to use opt-in for data tied to you. Being able to opt out afterwards isn't the same as being asked.
Look for anything that leaves Stoat
Bridges, outside AI services and image-scanning APIs send your messages or pictures off the platform. Check the policy says so and lets you choose.
